name: level1-win-efficient
description: Level 1 (Dusty Hollow): named for an efficient $80k win, no vehicle ever bought -- but #553 makes drill_hole a queued, vehicle-gated action, so drilling now costs real vehicle purchases where it previously cost none (still zero HAULING vehicles -- debris_hauler/rock_digger/rock_fragmenter/building_destroyer -- so 'no hauling infrastructure means no delivery ever succeeds' still holds). The real trajectory goes further than a missed $80k target: pattern 1 lands and blasts (killing its entire 4-person crew, exactly as tutorial-playthrough.json's own precedent), but the dead's permanently-zero morale (ScoreManager averages the whole roster, living and dead) drags wellbeing so low that pattern 2's fresh crew still walks the workforce out in a permanent revolt (WorkerRevolt.ts) before landing pattern 2's 25th hole -- see the Findings on the campaign status step for the full trajectory. The two survey steps (core_sample at (10,10), seismic at (20,20)) that gate the survey-confidence-overlay screenshot are untouched command-for-command, interaction-block-for-interaction-block from the version already confirmed via an inspected screenshot (not just source reading) to render the overlay genuinely -- the stale 'FAILS until GameRenderer wires survey overlay into syncFromContext()' warning this file previously carried is no longer true; a fresh interaction-mode run re-captures the same screenshots at whatever step index this longer file now gives them, not re-inspected as part of this #553 pass (command-mode only per this pass's own verification scope).

steps.description: #553: cash bumped from $50,000 to $3,000,000. This file's premise no longer holds 'no vehicle ever bought' as-is (drill_hole is now a queued, vehicle-gated action -- see Findings below), and the crew needed to work it is far larger than a single driller can sustain: sandbox-measured, six tier-3 drill_rig purchases across two patterns ($840,000 -- see Finding on tier choice below), six driller hires, and ~460 ticks of payroll/fuel/maintenance drain plus two punitive random events (lawsuit -$20,000, strike -$25,000) before the workforce permanently walks out. Sized generously above the sandbox-measured minimum rather than pared to the cent.

Left unmarked: hiring already grants the Rookie starting qualification (ROLE_STARTING_QUALIFICATION in Employee.ts); this only raises the level for the scenario's needs -- the player-facing path is `employee train`.

#553 Finding: surveyCount is 2 here, not the originally-declared 1 -- a pre-existing bug unrelated to #553 (confirmed red on this exact step even before any drilling change: `npx tsx scripts/run-all-scenarios.ts level1-win-efficient` on the unedited file fails here with 'surveyCount should be 1 but is 2'). Both the core_sample and seismic surveys queued at tick 0 finish within these 72 ticks (seismic at tick 41, core_sample at tick 69); the original count only ever matched by coincidence with a different RNG draw. Corrected here as part of re-deriving the file's real trajectory, per this batch's own convention.

#553: drill_hole is now a queued, vehicle-gated action -- a licensed driller must physically drive a drill_rig to each hole. This file's premise ('no vehicle ever bought') can no longer hold as literally stated; drilling now costs real vehicle purchases where it previously cost none. Employee #2, first of three drillers bought for pattern 1 (see Finding on crew size below).

#553: the drill_rig licence a driller needs before any drill_hole action can be claimed -- hiring only grants the role's own starting qualification (blasting), never a driving licence. Left unmarked for the same reason as the geology assign_skill above: the player-facing path is `employee train` at a driving_center.

#553 Finding (crew size): a lone driller-and-rig pair takes far longer than 'roughly 200-300 ticks' to land even the smallest of this file's three patterns -- sandbox-measured, a single tier-1 pair still has 0 of pattern 1's 16 holes landed by tick 245 (173 ticks in). The drill_rig and employee both spawn at the site's grid centre (~48,48 on this 96x96 map) regardless of where the pattern is, so every pair pays the same long march to (10,10) before drilling even starts; a lone worker collapses from fatigue repeatedly during that march, each collapse discarding the walk in progress (TaskDispatch.ts's interruptActiveAction releases the vehicle reservation). Employee #3, second of three.
Employee #4, third driller for pattern 1's 3-pair crew.

#553 Finding (tier choice): tier-1 drill_rigs (speed 1.0) were tried first, matching this batch's own template selector -- but even 5 tier-1 pairs left pattern 1's 16 holes undrilled through tick 790 in a sandbox probe (a genuine regression once more than a handful of pairs compete for the same claim pool, not just slow). Tier-3 rigs (speed 1.8x, VEHICLE_TIER_MULTIPLIERS in balance.ts) let 3 pairs land pattern 1 by tick 265, comfortably inside the wellbeing-zero-to-revolt window measured below -- the tier bump is what makes 3 pairs (not 6+) workable, at 4x tier-1's per-rig cost. `data-tier="3"` replaces this batch's usual `data-tier="1"` template for exactly this reason.

#553: does NOT re-click the vehicles toolbar tab -- the panel is already open (left that way by the previous buy/driver steps), and UIManager.togglePanel closes an ALREADY-active panel on re-click instead of leaving it open, which is exactly what made this step's own tier-3 button resolve to zero size before this fix (the panel itself went display:none, not a stale selector -- confirmed via a direct interaction-mode trace: step failed here with 'element has zero size (0x0)', while `getComputedStyle` on the button itself still reported its own authored display value, the signature of a hidden ancestor rather than a hidden element).

#553 Finding (real trajectory): the workforce permanently revolts (WorkerRevolt.ts, REVOLT_TICKS=120 consecutive ticks at wellBeing<=0) here, before pattern 2's 25 holes finish landing (10 of 25 still ordered) -- sandbox-measured across three independent tick-chunking styles (5/10/20-tick batches all agree). wellBeing first hit exactly 0 at tick 185, mid-pattern-1; ScoreManager's avgMorale averages ALL employees ever hired, including the dead (their morale sits permanently at 0, Employee.ts/events.ts), so each blast's casualties permanently drag the roster average down for the rest of the file -- pattern 1's 4 deaths are why pattern 2's own crew, freshly hired at full morale, still starts the drain already averaged toward zero. This -- not a third blast, not a near-breakeven $46,760 -- is the file's real ending under #553: buying enough automated drilling capacity to survive one blast does not leave enough workforce goodwill to survive a second.

#553 Findings, final: the level ends in a permanent worker revolt at tick 458, with pattern 2 abandoned 10 holes short of its 25. deathCount stays at 4 (all from blast 1) -- the revolt is a mass walkout, not a mass casualty (WorkerRevolt.ts never touches damage.deathCount), matching a direct trace through this exact sequence. Cash ends at $2,025,975, down from the $3,000,000 opening bump, spent on: 6 tier-3 drill_rigs ($840,000), 6 driller hires + 1 surveyor ($7,200), 386 ticks (72->458) of payroll/fuel/maintenance for a 4-to-7-person roster, and two punitive random events (an ore-name lawsuit -$20,000 at tick 130, a union strike -$25,000 at tick 278) -- no lucky_strike bonus landed this run, unlike the pre-#553 version of this file. Like every other file in this batch, no hauling vehicle (debris_hauler, rock_digger, rock_fragmenter, building_destroyer) is ever bought, so both accepted contracts sit at 0.0 kg stored the whole file and expire for their full penalty before pattern 2 even lands its third hole -- the file's other, narrower point ('no hauling infrastructure means no delivery ever succeeds') holds exactly as before. What #553 changes is the premise one level up: this was never going to be an efficient $80,000 win, and it is no longer even a survivable one -- automated drilling costs enough goodwill, on top of enough cash, that the workforce quits before a second pattern can fire.
